procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 2, 1965, in C.W.J.C. 442 of 1965; Judgment and order dated December 22, 1965, in Criminal Misc. Nos. 649, 666, 667, 668 and 669 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Patna High Court issued the orders that were challenged in the Supreme Court. One was in C.W.J.C. 442 of 1965, and the others were in Criminal Misc. Nos. 649, 666, 667, 668 and 669 of 1965.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court heard a Civil Appeal (No. 1971 of 1966) based on a petition under Art. 32 of the Constitution of India for the enforcement of fundamental rights, an appeal from the judgment and order dated December 2, 1965 of the Patna High Court in C.W.J.C. 442 of 1965, appeals by special leave from the judgment and order dated December 22, 1965 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Misc. Nos. 649, 666, 667, 668 and 669 of 1965, and Writ Petition Nos. 103 and 199 of 1967. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the petitions and appeals.

directions: C.A. No. 1971 of 1966, W.P. Nos. 199 and 103 of 1967 are dismissed with costs.
There will be one hearing fee.
Cr. As. Nos. 164-168 of 1966 are dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the State Government acted unreasonably in exercising its power under s. 4(1) by declaring a market area that was allegedly too wide for effective control or inconvenient for growers.

facts: The petitioner argued that the market area declared by the State Government under s. 4(1) of the Act was too wide.
law: The power of the State Government under s. 4(1) to declare a market area, after considering objections and suggestions, must be exercised reasonably.
application: The Court found that there was no material or evidence on the record to demonstrate that the government had acted unreasonably.
The petitioner failed to show that the market area was so wide that the market committee could not effectively control the sale and purchase of agricultural produce within it.
Similarly, there was no proof that the area was so large that it was inconvenient for growers to bring their produce to the market yards.
The Court noted that the government had followed the proper procedure by considering all objections and suggestions before declaring the market area.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the objection was not well-founded because there was no evidence to show that the State Government had acted unreasonably in declaring the size of the market area.

issue.issue_text: Whether a market was properly established, given the argument that a market must be a well-defined site with specific equipment and facilities, which the market committee had not provided.

facts: The party challenging the market's validity argued that the market committee had not established a proper market because it had not provided a well-defined physical site with specific equipment and facilities.
A notification had been issued under section 5(2) of the relevant Act, which fixed the boundaries of the 'market proper' and the 'market yards'.
There was no evidence to show that the market committee had refused to carry out any direction from the State Government to provide specific facilities.
law: Section 2(h) of the Act defines a 'market' as consisting of the 'market proper' and 'market yards'.
Section 2(k) and Section 5(2)(ii) define the 'market proper' as a larger designated area, not necessarily a specific site with buildings.
According to Section 5(2) and Rule 59(2), a market is legally 'established' by the issuance of a notification that fixes the boundaries of the market proper and market yards.
Section 18(i) requires the market committee to provide facilities as directed by the State Government.
Sections 28(2) and 30(i) permit, but do not oblige, the market committee to acquire and own land and buildings for the market.
application: The Court found that the argument that a market must be a physical site with equipment overlooked the Act's specific definition of a 'market'.
The Court explained that the law distinguishes between 'market yards' (which are defined enclosures) and the 'market proper' (which is a larger area).

The Court reasoned that the legal act of establishing a market is accomplished simply by issuing the official notification under Section 5(2) to define these areas. The physical construction of facilities is not a prerequisite for the market's legal establishment.

The Court addressed the issue of facilities by pointing to Section 18(i), noting that the committee's obligation is to provide facilities when directed by the government. Since there was no proof that the committee had failed to follow such a direction, this part of the argument failed.
The Court further clarified that while the committee has the power to acquire land, it is not legally required to do so to establish a market.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and held that the market was properly established. The legal establishment of a market is achieved through the formal notification defining its boundaries, and does not require the pre-existence of a specific physical site with equipment and facilities.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a market was properly established, given the argument that a market must be a well-defined site with specific equipment and facilities, which the market committee had not provided.
appellant_arguments: The market committee has not established a proper market.
A market must be a well-defined site equipped with market equipment and facilities.
respondent_arguments: The legal definition of a 'market' under s. 2(h) is broader than a single site; it consists of the 'market proper' (a larger area) and 'market yards' (well-defined enclosures).
A market is legally established simply by a declaration under s. 5(2) that fixes the boundaries of the market proper and market yards.
The market committee's duty under s. 18(i) is to provide facilities as directed by the State Government, and there is no evidence that the committee failed to carry out any such direction.
The committee is not always obligated to acquire and own lands and buildings for the market.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A state government does not violate constitutional equality provisions by implementing an act gradually in different parts of its territory. The legal establishment of a market under the relevant statute is accomplished by a formal declaration of its boundaries and does not require the prior existence of physical facilities. The government's power to declare a market area must be exercised reasonably, and the burden is on the challenger to prove that the designated area is unmanageably large or otherwise unreasonable.
obiter: A market committee must provide for such facilities in the market as the State Government may from time to time direct.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the State Government acted within its statutory authority and followed the prescribed procedures in establishing the market. The appellants failed to substantiate their claims with evidence, specifically regarding the unreasonableness of the market area's size and their incorrect assertion that a market must be a pre-equipped physical site rather than an area established by legal notification.
legal_tests_applied: The power of the State Government under s. 4(1) to declare a market area must be exercised reasonably.
A market is legally established by following the statutory procedure for issuing notifications that declare the market proper and market yards, as laid down in secs. 5 and 18(i) of the Act.
why_appellant_lost: Regarding the size of the market area, the appellant provided no material on the record to show that the Government acted unreasonably, that the market was too wide for effective control, or that it was inconvenient for growers.

The appellant's argument that a market must be a well-defined site with equipment was rejected, as the court found that the market was properly established simply by issuing notifications declaring the market proper and market yards in accordance with statutory procedure.
why_respondent_won: The court found that the market area was duly declared under s. 4(1) only after the government had considered all objections and suggestions, indicating a reasonable exercise of power.

The court affirmed that the market was legally established because the government had followed the procedure laid down in secs. 5, 18 (i) and r. 59 by issuing the required notifications for the market proper and market yards.
policy_considerations: The State Government is not obligated to implement the Act and its Rules in all parts of the state simultaneously; it is permissible to establish markets gradually and from time to time in different areas.
